title: What Really Happens to a Heat Pump at 0°F

sentences.text: Picture the coldest night of a northern winter: frost on the windows, and the heat pump outside still humming.
sentences.note: A scene with no figure and no claim about what the heat pump does.

sentences.text: Is it still heating the house, or has it turned into a very expensive space heater?
Meters, not marketing, can settle this.
An NH Patch headline put the doubt bluntly: "Taxpayers On The Hook For Tech That Falls Flat In The Cold".

assertions.text: An NH Patch headline said heat pumps are tech that falls flat in the cold.

quote.text: Taxpayers On The Hook For Tech That Falls Flat In The Cold
quote.speaker: NH Patch

sentences.text: The Mass Save heat pump page answers that "many provide efficient heat at outdoor temperatures as low as -15 °F".

assertions.text: Mass Save says of heat pumps: "many provide efficient heat at outdoor temperatures as low as -15 °F".

quote.text: many provide efficient heat at outdoor temperatures as low as -15 °F
quote.speaker: Mass Save

sentences.text: So does a heat pump give up in the cold, or carry on as if nothing happened?
Start with the bluntest question: does the heat keep coming at all?
Engineers score heating efficiency as a COP, and plain electric resistance heat scores 1.

assertions.text: Electric resistance heat operates at a COP of 1, less efficient than a heat pump.
qualifications: s11 says non-cold-climate models ran less efficiently in the cold, and s19 how far COP falls; the claim is not that every unit beats resistance heat.

sentences.text: In one evaluation, engineers metered the heat that dozens of ductless mini-splits delivered over back-to-back winters, and in the later one the units averaged a COP of 1.5 between -10 and 0 °F.

assertions.text: An evaluation metered delivered heat from dozens of ductless mini-splits over winter 2015 and winter 2016; in the 2016 winter their COPs averaged 1.5 at -10 to 0 °F.
qualifications: s10 says the first winter, with deep snow and ice around the outdoor units, went less efficiently.
s11 says the sample included non-cold-climate models.

sentences.text: That is 50 percent more heat per unit of electricity than resistance heat, which the evaluators called far superior; in the earlier winter, with deep snow and ice around the outdoor units, the units ran less efficiently.

assertions.text: At a COP of 1.5 the mini-splits gave effective heating efficiencies 50% higher than electric resistance heating, which the evaluators called far superior.
The units operated less efficiently in winter 2015, which had prolonged deep snow and cold, with snow and ice around outdoor units, than in winter 2016.
qualifications: The sentence carries the first winter as the weaker result beside the figure.

sentences.text: And not only the cold-climate models: the ordinary ones in that evaluation also ran below 0 °F, just less efficiently.

assertions.text: In the evaluation, observed non-cold-climate models operated at outdoor temperatures below 0 °F, at lower efficiency than cold-climate models.
qualifications: The sentence says they ran less efficiently than the cold-climate models.

sentences.text: A newer field test followed prototype cold-climate heat pumps, and leaving out the periods when backup heat or defrost was running, their median COP between 0 and 5 °F was 1.9.

assertions.text: Excluding periods with auxiliary heat or defrost, the prototype cold-climate heat pumps in the field had a median COP of 1.9 in the 0 to 5 °F bin.
qualifications: The sentence says the figure leaves out backup heat and defrost periods, and that the units were prototypes.
s13 says the prototypes did better in the lab than in the field.

sentences.text: Those prototypes tested better in the lab, but in the field most still beat 1.75, the COP the EPA's Energy Star label requires of a cold-climate heat pump at 5 °F.

assertions.text: The prototypes' laboratory performance was significantly more efficient, but most units' observed field COP was above 1.75, the EPA Energy Star requirement for cold-climate heat pumps at 5 °F.
qualifications: The sentence says the lab results were better than the field and that most units, not all, cleared 1.75.

sentences.text: So the heat keeps coming. But efficiency is only half of it.
As the channel Technology Connections puts it, "along with getting less efficient, their actual heat output also drops."

assertions.text: Technology Connections said that along with getting less efficient, heat pumps' actual heat output also drops.

quote.text: along with getting less efficient, their actual heat output also drops.
quote.speaker: Technology Connections

sentences.text: In northern Minnesota, researchers watched one small ductless unit hold a steady median output from 10 °F all the way down to -15 °F.

assertions.text: One 1-ton ductless heat pump in Northern Minnesota delivered a consistent median capacity from 10 °F to -15 °F.
qualifications: The sentence says it was one unit.
s17 and s18 give its reduced output below -15 °F and the researchers' advice to keep backup there.

sentences.text: Below that it kept running at reduced output, and at -20 °F and colder it delivered only about 20 percent of what it was rated for at 5 °F.

assertions.text: The unit continued to operate from -15 °F to -25 °F at reduced capacity; between -20 and -25 °F its median delivered capacity was approximately 20% of its rated capacity at 5 °F.
qualifications: The sentence names the ductless unit and its rated 5 °F output; the UK trial that did not report capacity is not cited here.

sentences.text: The researchers' verdict was that units like it should not be used without backup below -15 °F.

assertions.text: The researchers concluded the reduction in capacity shows these units should not be used without backup at extreme temperatures below -15 °F.
qualifications: This sentence is the qualification on s16.

sentences.text: Efficiency follows the same slope: in the same Minnesota research, outdoor temperature had the biggest effect on COP, and heat-pump-only cycles managed only around 1.3 at 10 °F, less than half what they reached on mild days.

assertions.text: In the Minnesota study, outdoor air temperature had the largest impact on COP; heat-pump-only heating events had COPs around 1.3 at 10 °F, rising to around 3.0 to 4.5 in the shoulder heating seasons (around 50 to 60 °F), so 1.3 is less than half of the mild-weather figure.
qualifications: The sentence names the Minnesota research and its heat-pump-only cycles; the UK trial's smaller fall in COP is a different fleet and is not cited here.

sentences.note: CEE 2017 and CEE 2018 are one study (sameStudyAs), so the script calls it the same Minnesota research. "Less than half": 1.3 against around 3.0 to 4.5.

sentences.text: Then there is the frost.
In cold, humid air, frost builds up on the outdoor coil, and to melt it the heat pump runs in reverse, pulling heat out of the house, which can cool the air coming out of the vents.

assertions.text: In cold, humid conditions frost accumulates on the outdoor coil and cuts heat exchange; defrost reverses the refrigerant flow so the heat pump rejects heat from the conditioned space to melt the frost, which can drop the supply air temperature.

sentences.text: In the prototype field test, defrost used a median of 5 to 8 percent of the energy at the temperatures where it cost most, a small share, though one site spent 16 percent of its time in defrost.

assertions.text: Defrost was most energy intensive at 5 to 35 °F, where the median share of energy expended was between 5% and 8%, a small portion; one site spent 16% of its time in defrost under 40 °F against an overall average of 5%.

sentences.text: Which brings us to the real catch: backup heat.
When a heat pump's electric backup strips kick in, Jordan Dearden warns, "They'll also absolutely destroy your electric bill."

assertions.text: Jordan Dearden said electric backup heat strips will absolutely destroy your electric bill.

quote.text: They'll also absolutely destroy your electric bill.
quote.speaker: Jordan Dearden

sentences.text: In the prototype test, the units ran mostly on the heat pump alone, even at the lowest temperatures, and backup-only operation was minimal above 0 °F.

assertions.text: The units primarily operated in heat-pump-only mode even at the lowest outdoor temperatures, and auxiliary-only operation was minimal above 0 °F.
qualifications: s26 gives how often backup ran below 0 °F.

sentences.text: But in the coldest range with enough data, below 0 °F, backup elements were on 25 percent of the time, and only some of the 22 sites had enough data that cold.

assertions.text: In the coldest outdoor temperature bins with sufficient data (-10 to 0 °F), auxiliary elements were engaged 25% of the time across sites; the two coldest bins had a sample of 8 and 11 of the 22 sites.
qualifications: The sentence says only some of the sites had data that cold.
s31 and s41 say how much backup runs depends on sizing and controls.
These are the 22 field-test sites; the Maine whole-home study found backup there was mostly fossil fuel and resistance backup rare, and this sentence does not generalise beyond its sites.

sentences.text: Some backup use came from the thermostat: backup heat began at around 30 to 35 °F, and the researchers expect it would start much lower without homeowners changing setpoints, or with smarter thermostat controls.

assertions.text: Switchover to supplemental heat was observed around 30 to 35 °F; the researchers say a typical switchover temperature without homeowner setpoint interference, or with better setpoint controls, would likely be much lower.
qualifications: s18 says the ductless unit needs backup below -15 F; this sentence only reports when backup switched on and why.

sentences.text: Some came from faults: two sites fired up higher stages of backup heat during defrost, at least one did it in normal heating too, and the manufacturer called that a controls problem.

assertions.text: Two sites engaged higher stages of auxiliary heat during defrost; at least one did so in normal operation too, which the manufacturer team said was a controls problem and not intended operation.

sentences.text: In the Minnesota study's all-electric system, the resistance booster joined in below 30 °F, yet because the heat pump ran first, the whole system still beat plain resistance heat even at the coldest reading, around -7 °F.

assertions.text: In the all-electric system, events with electric resistance booster heat occurred below 30 °F, but because the heat pump was prioritized, system COPs were greater than 1.0 even at the coldest outdoor temperature, around -7 °F.
qualifications: The sentence says the booster joined in and the system COP stayed above resistance heat, not that backup cost nothing.

sentences.text: In another field study, one site's compressor would not run below 0 °F at all, even with its lockout disabled, most likely because of an on-board control setting that cannot be adjusted in the field.

assertions.text: At Site 10 the compressor did not run below 0 °F although its lockout temperature was disabled, likely due to an on-board control setting that cannot be adjusted in the field.
qualifications: This sentence is the limitation on claims that cold-climate units keep heating below 0 °F.

sentences.text: Sizing matters too: one study estimated that in Minnesota a high-efficiency heat pump sized for the full heating load cut median bills by $182 a year, while one sized for the cooling load raised them by $96, because it leaned harder on electric resistance backup.

assertions.text: In Minnesota, median bill savings were $182/year for high-efficiency ASHPs sized for the heating load, while median bills rose $96/year when they were sized for the cooling load, because of higher use of electric resistance backup.
qualifications: The sentence says these are estimates and that the bill rise comes from sizing, not from cold-climate units as such.

sentences.text: So what does all this do to the bill?
For the Minnesota homes, which had heated with propane or electricity, the researchers used performance maps and typical Minnesota weather to estimate cost savings of 30 to 56 percent.

assertions.text: For Minnesota homes replacing propane furnaces or electric heating, performance maps, home heating loads and normalized Minnesota weather were used to estimate homeowner cost savings of 30% to 56%.
qualifications: The sentence names the baseline (propane or electric heat) and says the savings are estimated.

sentences.text: Gas is harder to beat: at the prices of those winters, the mini-splits from the first evaluation cost less to run than an 80 percent efficient gas system only above 70 °F, which the evaluators said made them no direct replacement for gas.

assertions.text: For natural gas, the cost breakpoint was above 70 °F in either winter, so the mini-splits only operated cost-effectively above 70 °F compared with an 80% efficient heating system, and the evaluators said they do not provide a viable direct replacement for a gas-fired system at those energy prices.
qualifications: The sentence ties the result to the prices of those winters.

sentences.text: Against propane, they were cheaper at every temperature.

assertions.text: The balance point for propane was -15 °F in both winters, meaning the mini-split was always less expensive than propane.

sentences.text: Even the measured units listed as cold-climate broke even with gas only above 58 °F; on paper, the rating curve of a then-current cold-climate model brought it down to between 28 and 40 °F.

assertions.text: For the measured units listed as cold climate units, gas balance points were above 58 °F for both winters; based on the rating curve of a current cold-climate unit with an HSPF of 13, the natural gas balance point dropped to 40 °F for 2015 and 28 °F for 2016.
qualifications: The sentence gives the measured cold-climate result first and says the 28 to 40 °F range is from a rating curve, on paper.

sentences.text: A cost model for Toronto and Edmonton that counts equipment as well as energy points the same way: in Toronto, standard heat pumps with gas backup came out the lowest-cost option for nearly all households, but in Edmonton that held only for some house types, and gas with air conditioning won the rest.

assertions.text: In Toronto, standard heat pumps with gas backup are the lowest-cost option for nearly all households under mid-range assumptions; in Edmonton they are the lowest-cost option for single family homes and townhouses built in 1940 or 1980, and in other cases gas and air conditioning is the most cost-competitive option.
qualifications: The sentence says the model counts equipment as well as energy (lifetime cost, per the verdict note) and limits it to the two cities and to the house types it found.

sentences.note: The verdict note on the cited passage says the model compares lifetime cost including equipment, not running cost alone; the sentence says so.

sentences.text: The model's reasons were cheap gas and the cold itself, which makes heat pumps less efficient and calls on the backup more.

assertions.text: Edmonton's result was due to low gas prices and climate conditions; the cold climate makes heat pumps relatively less efficient and results in greater use of the backup heating system.

sentences.text: So do heat pumps still work when it gets really cold?
In these field tests most units did: they kept heating below zero, with less efficiency and less output, and still got more heat from each unit of electricity than resistance heat.

assertions.text: Most metered mini-splits kept heating at -10 to 0 °F, and a ductless cold-climate unit kept operating down to -25 °F; not every unit did (one field site's compressor did not run below 0 °F).
qualifications: The sentence says most units, not all; s30 gives the site whose compressor did not run below 0 °F.
s44 says each test followed a limited number of units.

assertions.text: Their efficiency and output fell as it got colder.
qualifications: The sentence speaks of the field tests the video cites (s17 for output, s19 for COP); s44 says each followed a limited number of units.

assertions.text: Their COP stayed above that of electric resistance heat in the cold.
qualifications: s11 says ordinary models ran less efficiently in the cold and s19 how far COP falls; this sentence speaks of the field-tested units.

sentences.text: The catch is backup heat, which ran more as it got colder, and more where a unit was sized for cooling or its controls misbehaved.

assertions.text: Auxiliary heater usage generally increased at colder temperature bins.
A heat pump sized for the cooling load used more electric resistance backup.
A controls problem made at least one site engage higher stages of auxiliary heat.

sentences.text: And do they still save money?

Against propane or electric heat, the studies here say yes on running costs, though the Minnesota researchers put retrofit paybacks at over 10 years unless the old system needs replacing; against gas, it turns on the unit, the climate and local prices, and for the mini-splits measured in the first evaluation, gas won.

assertions.text: Against propane furnaces or electric heating, the Minnesota study estimated cost savings, though for retrofits paybacks will typically be longer than 10 years unless equipment replacement is necessary; and the mini-splits were always cheaper than propane.
qualifications: The sentence carries the Minnesota retrofit payback limit beside the savings.

assertions.text: Against gas, the result varied with the unit (measured units vs a rated cold-climate unit), the climate and gas prices (Toronto vs Edmonton), and for the measured mini-splits gas was cheaper below 70 °F.
qualifications: s34 ties the measured mini-splits result to the prices of those winters.

sentences.text: Each of these field tests followed a limited number of units, so they show what heat pumps can do in the cold, not what every installation will.

assertions.text: The field tests followed limited samples: dozens of metered mini-splits, 22 prototype sites, and one ductless unit for the coldest readings.

sentences.text: If your winters bite, ask the installer whether the unit is a cold-climate model, and whether it is sized for your heating load or only for your cooling.
sentences.note: Advice that points back to s16-s18 and s31; no new fact.

sentences.text: Ask what temperature the backup is set to start at, then keep the thermostat steady and watch how often the backup comes on.
sentences.note: Points back to s27 (setpoint changes raised the switchover temperature).

sentences.text: And if you heat with gas, work out the break-even temperature at your own prices before you decide what the furnace is for.
sentences.note: Points back to s34-s36; no figure.
